plan.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) weight loss in the randomized trials: how much people lost on average in SURMOUNT-1 (adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes, 72 weeks), how much it varied between people, why people with type 2 diabetes lost less on average (SURMOUNT-2, a separate trial), what share of the loss was lean mass, and the habits linked to getting the most from it
plan.angle: Tirzepatide weight loss in the trials, explained honestly. SURMOUNT-1 (adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes, 72 weeks) gives each dose arm against placebo with its per-arm n, 'counting everyone who started', plus the shares of people reaching 5%, 15% and 20%. Chapter 3 shows the spread between people, labelled 'about'. Chapter 4 covers SURMOUNT-2, a separate trial and not head-to-head (adults with obesity or overweight and type 2 diabetes, 72 weeks, 10 mg and 15 mg arms against their own placebo): say only that people with type 2 diabetes tend to lose less and that the paper doesn't establish why. Chapter 5 covers the DXA substudy (n=160, tirzepatide doses pooled against placebo): about three-quarters of the weight lost was fat and about a quarter was lean mass, the same split seen on placebo, and lean mass isn't pure muscle. Chapter 6 covers recommended habits (protein at each meal unless your clinician limits it, muscle-strengthening at least 2 days a week, started gently), never presented as proven on tirzepatide. Chapter 7 gives questions to ask your prescriber. Weight is one health measure among many.

plan.why:
Playbook long-form queue #3. Broad question with strong search demand (broad videos: median 621 min vs about 39 for narrow). Built only on settled primary sources (NEJM SURMOUNT-1, Lancet SURMOUNT-2, the Zepbound PI), so it can pass fact-check the first time. No overlap with the dropped Mounjaro vs Zepbound video or today's Shorts. | fact-check: This is a strong evergreen topic with real search demand, and it fits the GLP-1 pillar. The evidence base is solid: SURMOUNT-1 (NEJM 2022), SURMOUNT-2 (Lancet 2023), Zepbound PI Section 14, and the SURMOUNT-1 DXA body-composition paper (Look et al., Diabetes Obes Metab 2025, doi 10.1111/dom.16275, PMC11965027). I confirmed the DXA paper exists, and its figures match. It had 160 participants with DXA at baseline and week 72. At week 72, body weight changed by -21.3%, fat mass by -33.9% and lean mass by -10.9% on tirzepatide. On placebo the changes were -5.3%, -8.2% and -2.6%. About 75% of the weight lost was fat and about 25% was lean mass. That split was the same for tirzepatide and placebo.

Three things in the brief need changing:
1. Chapter 5 asks for 'per-arm substudy sizes'. The DXA paper reports tirzepatide doses pooled against placebo (n=160 in total). Don't invent per-dose DXA sizes. Report the pooled tirzepatide n and the placebo n exactly as the paper prints them.
2. Chapter 5 must also say the ~3:1 fat-to-lean split was the same on placebo. If it doesn't, viewers will read the split as something specific to tirzepatide. Keep 'lean mass isn't pure muscle' (it also includes water, organs and so on). Don't claim the lean-mass loss is harmless or harmful: the paper didn't measure function.
3. Chapter 4: SURMOUNT-2 doesn't establish why people with type 2 diabetes lose less. At most, say the paper notes that weight loss is generally lower in people with type 2 diabetes, and that the reasons aren't fully established. Don't name mechanisms (for example glucose-lowering drugs or less glucose lost in urine) unless the paper's text says them. SURMOUNT-2 tested only the 10 mg and 15 mg arms. Never put SURMOUNT-1 and SURMOUNT-2 numbers side by side on one stat card.

Other checks:
- Saying the dose arm labels (5/10/15 mg) as trial arms is acceptable under the dosing rule, as long as each one is framed as a trial arm and comes with 'your prescriber decides yours'. Don't show any titration schedule or timeline.
- Chapter 3's spread: use only the distributions the paper or its supplement shows, labelled 'about'. Don't frame them as 'non-responders' or make predictions.
- Chapter 6 habits are general recommendations from the 2025 advisory and WHO. Never present them as trial findings.
- Keep the GI line exactly as written, and keep the don't-stop and prescriber lines.

package.description:
How much weight did people lose on tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound)?

Quick answer: in SURMOUNT-1 (adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes, 72 weeks), average weight loss was 20.9% on the 15 mg arm vs 3.1% on placebo, counting everyone who started. On that arm, 57% lost a fifth or more (placebo: 3%). In a separate trial, SURMOUNT-2 (adults with obesity or overweight and type 2 diabetes), average losses were smaller.

script.hook_pattern: Stakes + specificity: sentence 1 asks the title question with the drug named. The headline SURMOUNT-1 number lands by about 13 s, and a second concrete payoff (57% lost at least a fifth) comes at 15–30 s. Then a 'you' scenario and a one-sentence open loop (placebo's fat-to-lean split), paid off in the 'Fat or muscle?' chapter.

visual.stock_query: curious person facing scale question mark

scenes.retention_device: Title question asked in sentence 1 (curiosity gap)

scenes.narration: In the SURMOUNT-1 trial, people on the 15 milligram arm lost an average of 20.9 percent of their body weight. That was over 72 weeks.

scenes.retention_device: Short answer delivered by about 13 s

scenes.narration: On placebo, the average loss was 3.1 percent. Everyone in the trial was an adult with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes.

visual.stat_label: SURMOUNT-1 placebo arm, average loss, 72 weeks

scenes.narration: Here's a second number. On that same 15 milligram arm, 57 percent of people lost at least a fifth of their body weight. On placebo, 3 percent did.
But you're the one holding the pen, and you want to know where you might land.

visual.stock_query: thoughtful person kitchen table pen box

scenes.narration: Picture someone like Dana, 48, imagined for this video. A few months in, her scale moved fast, then slowed, and a friend on the same medicine is losing faster.

visual.stock_query: worried woman comparing phone and scale

scenes.narration: Stick around for the fat-or-muscle chapter, because placebo shows something about that lost weight that's easy to miss.
scenes.on_screen_text: Fat or muscle? Wait for it
scenes.retention_device: Single-sentence open loop, paid off in 'Fat or muscle?'

scenes.narration: First, what 'average' really means. Then how much people varied, why diabetes changes things, and the habits experts recommend alongside it.
So who exactly is the 'average' in a trial like this?

visual.stock_query: chapter card crowd of people counted

scenes.narration: Quick note first. Mounjaro and Zepbound are both tirzepatide. In the US, Zepbound is approved for chronic weight management, and Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes.
SURMOUNT-1 randomly assigned 2,539 adults to one of four groups, for 72 weeks.

visual.stock_query: large diverse crowd split four groups

scenes.narration: 630 people got the 5 milligram arm. 636 got 10 milligrams. 630 got 15 milligrams. And 643 got placebo.

visual.stock_query: four groups of people labelled arms

scenes.narration: Those are trial arms, not a plan for you. Your prescriber decides yours.

visual.stock_query: doctor and patient friendly clinic chat

scenes.narration: Here's a detail that changes how you read the results. Every group, placebo included, also got regular lifestyle counselling, with a reduced-calorie eating plan and physical activity goals.

visual.stock_query: counsellor with meal plan and sneakers

scenes.narration: So the placebo group wasn't doing nothing. Their 3.1 percent loss is roughly what counselling plus a dummy injection achieved here.

visual.fact: Placebo + lifestyle counselling: −3.1% average at 72 weeks
visual.stock_query: placebo character walking with meal plan

scenes.narration: And the main numbers count everyone who started, including people who stopped their injections early. That's a stricter way to report results, and closer to real life.

visual.stock_query: everyone in crowd gets tally mark

scenes.narration: So, counting everyone, here's each arm at 72 weeks. On the 5 milligram arm, the average loss was 15 percent.

visual.stat_label: Tirzepatide 5 mg arm, average loss, 72 weeks

scenes.narration: On the 10 milligram arm, the average loss was 19.5 percent.

visual.stat_label: Tirzepatide 10 mg arm, average loss, 72 weeks

scenes.narration: On the 15 milligram arm, it was 20.9 percent. And on placebo, 3.1 percent.

visual.stock_query: four bars side by side chart

scenes.narration: To make that concrete: for someone starting at 100 kilograms, about 220 pounds, a 20.9 percent loss would be about 21 kilograms. That's roughly 46 pounds. Just arithmetic, not a prediction.

visual.stock_query: calculator next to bag of flour

scenes.narration: But an average is just one dot on a chart, and real people are scattered around it. So how far apart were they?

visual.stock_query: one dot among scattered dots chart

scenes.narration: If the average on the top arm was about a fifth, did everyone lose about a fifth?
No. The paper reports what share of people crossed each line, and the spread is wide.
Start with a loss of at least 5 percent. On the tirzepatide arms, 85 to 91 percent of people reached it, depending on the arm. On placebo, 35 percent did.

visual.stat_label: Lost ≥5%: tirzepatide arms vs placebo, 72 weeks
visual.stock_query: many characters stepping over first line

scenes.narration: Flip that around. On the 15 milligram arm, roughly 1 in 10 people didn't reach a 5 percent loss, even after 72 weeks.

visual.stock_query: ten figures one standing apart calmly

scenes.retention_device: Surprising flip of the same data

scenes.narration: Next line: a loss of at least 15 percent. That was about 48 percent of people on the 5 milligram arm, about 67 percent on 10, and about 71 percent on 15. On placebo, fewer than 1 in 10.
And a loss of at least 20 percent: about 30 percent of people on 5 milligrams, 50 percent on 10, and 57 percent on 15. On placebo, 3 percent.
Now picture ten people from the 15 milligram arm around one table. Five or six lost a fifth or more. One didn't reach 5 percent. The rest landed in between.

visual.stock_query: ten diverse people around dinner table

scenes.narration: If your loss is slower than someone else's, that's not a willpower verdict. People on the exact same arm, with the same counselling, had very different results.
This trial wasn't built to predict who loses what, so these shares describe groups, not your personal future.

visual.stock_query: group photo frame not crystal ball

scenes.narration: Back to Dana and her faster friend. Same medicine, different bodies. The trial shows gaps like that between people on the same arm. It's not proof Dana is doing anything wrong.

visual.stock_query: two friends walking different paces smiling

scenes.narration: But one group lost noticeably less on average, and it got its own trial.
So does having type 2 diabetes change how much weight people lose on tirzepatide?

visual.stock_query: chapter card blood sugar meter friendly

scenes.narration: That was tested in SURMOUNT-2. It's a separate trial with different people, so it's not a head-to-head with SURMOUNT-1.

visual.stock_query: two trial folders on separate tables

scenes.narration: It enrolled 938 adults with obesity or overweight and type 2 diabetes, for 72 weeks. 312 got the 10 milligram arm, 311 got 15 milligrams, and 315 got placebo.

items: Adults with obesity or overweight + type 2 diabetes
visual.stock_query: three groups of adults with clipboards

scenes.narration: Counting everyone who started, the average loss on the 10 milligram arm was 12.8 percent.
On the 15 milligram arm, it was 14.7 percent. On placebo, 3.2 percent.
And 79 to 83 percent of people on the tirzepatide arms lost at least 5 percent of their weight, compared with 32 percent on placebo.
So people with type 2 diabetes tend to lose less on average, across weight-loss trials in general. Why? The reasons aren't fully established.

visual.stock_query: calm scientist beside open question mark

scenes.narration: So we won't guess. If you have type 2 diabetes, ask your prescriber what this trial means for you, because your full picture matters more than any average.
scenes.on_screen_text: Ask what it means for you

scenes.narration: Now, the chapter I promised at the start. When the scale drops by a fifth, what exactly is leaving the body?
scenes.retention_device: Return to main open loop before chapter change

scenes.narration: How much of the weight lost on tirzepatide was fat, and how much was lean mass?

visual.stock_query: chapter card fat and muscle icons

scenes.narration: Inside SURMOUNT-1, 160 people had DXA scans. That's a low-dose X-ray scan that separates fat from lean tissue. They were scanned at the start and at week 72.

visual.stat_label: SURMOUNT-1 participants with DXA body scans

scenes.narration: The three tirzepatide doses were pooled together and compared with placebo.

visual.stock_query: three jars poured into one jar

scenes.narration: On tirzepatide, body weight fell by 21.3 percent in this group.

visual.stat_label: DXA group, tirzepatide pooled: weight, 72 weeks

scenes.narration: Fat mass fell by about a third. That's 33.9 percent of the fat people started with.
Lean mass fell too. That drop was 10.9 percent.
Put those together, and about three-quarters of the weight lost was fat. About a quarter was lean mass.

visual.stat_label: Fat to lean, share of weight lost

scenes.narration: Now here's the part that's easy to miss. People on placebo lost less, 5.3 percent of body weight. But their split was the same. About three-quarters fat, about a quarter lean.

visual.myth: That lean-mass share is a tirzepatide thing
visual.fact: Placebo showed the same ~3:1 fat-to-lean split
visual.stock_query: two matching pie charts side by side

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the main open loop

scenes.narration: So that ratio isn't unique to tirzepatide. In this study, it's what weight loss looked like in both groups.
One more thing. Lean mass isn't pure muscle. It also includes water, organs and other tissue that isn't fat.
And this body-scan study didn't directly measure strength or physical performance. So it can't tell us whether that lean loss is harmful or harmless. Anyone who's certain is going past the data.

visual.stock_query: neutral mascot beside blank strength meter

scenes.narration: For Dana, that's useful, not scary. The goal isn't to fear lean loss. It's to give her muscles good reasons to stay. And that's where habits come in.
scenes.on_screen_text: Give muscle a reason to stay
scenes.retention_device: Thread return plus bridge into next chapter

scenes.narration: So what can you actually do to protect muscle while you lose weight?

visual.stock_query: chapter card protein plate and band

scenes.narration: An honesty check first. SURMOUNT-1 didn't test a protein target or strength training. These are general recommendations from expert groups, not proven tirzepatide results.
A 2025 joint advisory on nutrition alongside GLP-1 medicines emphasizes getting enough protein and doing strength training.

visual.stock_query: advisory document with protein and dumbbell

scenes.narration: Habit one: include a protein source at each meal, unless your clinician has told you to limit protein, for example because of kidney disease.
When your appetite is smaller, eating the protein part of your plate first is one simple way to keep it from getting crowded out.

visual.stock_query: small plate fork reaching for salmon

scenes.narration: Habit two: muscle-strengthening activity on at least 2 days a week, working all the major muscle groups. That's the World Health Organization's recommendation for adults.

Start gently. Sit-to-stands from a chair, wall push-ups or resistance bands all count, and the WHO says some activity is better than none. If you have a heart, joint or other condition, check with your clinician first.

visual.stock_query: person doing wall push-ups at home

scenes.narration: Picture Dana. Two mornings a week, ten minutes of chair stands and band rows. Eggs or yogurt at breakfast. Not heroic. Just repeatable.

visual.stock_query: woman doing band rows living room

scenes.narration: But the most useful habit might not happen at home at all. It happens in a short conversation with your prescriber.
So what's worth asking the person who prescribes it?
Start with side effects. In SURMOUNT-1, the most common were stomach-related, like nausea, diarrhea and constipation. They happened mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time.
In SURMOUNT-1, 2.6 percent of people on placebo stopped because of side effects. On the tirzepatide arms, it was 4.3 to 7.1 percent.

visual.stat_label: Stopped for side effects: tirzepatide vs placebo

scenes.narration: If you get severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting, get medical help right away.
scenes.on_screen_text: Severe stomach pain? Get help right away

scenes.narration: For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own. Talk to your prescriber.
Here are five questions worth bringing. One: what would a good result look like for me, beyond the scale? Two: does type 2 diabetes, or anything else I have, change what to expect?

Tirzepatide is a prescription medicine, so talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

scenes.narration: So, how much weight can you lose on tirzepatide? In SURMOUNT-1, in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes, average losses ran from 15 percent to 20.9 percent across the arms over 72 weeks. Placebo: 3.1 percent.

People varied widely. In a separate trial of adults with type 2 diabetes, average losses were smaller. And in a body-scan study of 160 SURMOUNT-1 participants, about a quarter of the weight lost was lean mass, on tirzepatide and placebo alike.

factcheck.summary:
This passes. Every key number I could open a source for matches it. SURMOUNT-1 (NEJM, July 2022): 2,539 adults; average loss −15.0%, −19.5% and −20.9% on the 5, 10 and 15 mg arms vs −3.1% on placebo at 72 weeks; 50% and 57% lost ≥20% vs 3% on placebo; stomach side effects mostly during dose escalation. SURMOUNT-2 (Lancet, August 2023): 938 adults; −12.8% and −14.7% vs −3.2%; 79.2% and 82.8% lost ≥5% vs 32.5% on placebo. The DXA body-scan study (Look et al., DOM, 2025): 160 people; weight −21.3% vs −5.3%; fat mass −33.9%; lean mass −10.9%; about 75% fat and 25% lean in both groups; strength and physical performance were not measured directly. The 2025 joint advisory (AJCN, PMID 40450457) is real and recommends resistance training. The WHO 2020 guideline is real.

Several other numbers are consistent with the published trial but I couldn't read them directly, because PubMed showed a cookie wall and both Lilly PDFs (S4, S5) wouldn't convert to text. These are: the per-arm sizes in both trials, the ≥5% (85–91%) and ≥15% (48%, 67%, 71%) shares, the 30% figure for 5 mg at ≥20%, and the 4.3–7.1% vs 2.6% who stopped for side effects. The same goes for the WHO wording (2+ days of muscle-strengthening; some activity is better than none), the advisory's protein-at-each-meal point, the "decreased over time" wording, and the S4/S5 revision dates (28 and 27 Aug 2026). The pipeline's own fixed figures confirm those revision dates and the "mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time" wording.

Safety and framing are solid. The trial population is named correctly. The video warns against comparing trials head-to-head and says the results describe groups, not predictions. It has caveats for kidney disease and heart or joint conditions, the exact emergency line with the don't-stop line after it, the prescriber line, and the watch-next close. Dana is clearly labelled as imagined and isn't shamed.

There are four minor scope and attribution tweaks below, each with a copy-paste fix.

issues.claim: And about a quarter of the weight lost was lean mass, on tirzepatide and placebo alike.
issues.problem: The recap drops the scope. The 75/25 split comes from a 160-person DXA body-scan study inside SURMOUNT-1, not the whole trial. The on-screen card has the same problem.
issues.fix: Narration: "And in a body-scan study of 160 SURMOUNT-1 participants, about a quarter of the weight lost was lean mass, on tirzepatide and placebo alike." On-screen list item 3: "~1/4 lean mass in SURMOUNT-1 DXA scans (n=160), tirzepatide and placebo"

issues.claim: The paper notes that weight loss is generally lower in people with type 2 diabetes, and the reasons aren't fully established.
issues.problem: The SURMOUNT-2 abstract doesn't say this, and I couldn't open the full text to find the sentence. The general point is well established, but the quote-like attribution to 'the paper' isn't verified.
issues.fix: "So people with type 2 diabetes tend to lose less on average, across weight-loss trials in general. Why? The reasons aren't fully established."

issues.claim: These habits weren't tested in SURMOUNT-1.
issues.problem: This seems to clash with s14, which says everyone in the trial got physical activity goals and a reduced-calorie eating plan. What wasn't tested is a protein target or strength training specifically.
issues.fix: "An honesty check first. SURMOUNT-1 didn't test a protein target or strength training. These are general recommendations from expert groups, not proven tirzepatide results."

issues.claim: And the study didn't measure strength or physical function.
issues.problem: This is true of the DXA body-scan study. But SURMOUNT-1 as a whole did collect self-reported physical function (SF-36), so 'the study' is ambiguous.
issues.fix: "And this body-scan study didn't directly measure strength or physical performance. So it can't tell us whether that lean loss is harmful or harmless."

The pose is static across all three frames (0.0s, 1.1s, 2.7s) with only the question-mark icon's position wobbling slightly — low visual energy for the hook.

issues: big number alone is less emotionally compelling than a fear/question hook
heart icon mismatches the weight-loss topic, risking confusion with a heart-health video

thumbnail.reasoning: All three are legible at phone size with short, uncut text and no answer given away. #0 "FAT OR MUSCLE?" pairs a strong, title-relevant curiosity gap (a common fear among GLP-1 users—losing muscle, not just fat) with a worried, sweating face that matches the tension of the question, and a clean single focal point (the scale character). #1 "72 WEEKS" is clear and credible but a bare number is a weaker emotional hook than a direct question tied to a relatable fear. #2 "WHY SO DIFFERENT?" has a worried face that fits its question, but the heart icon is visually mismatched with a weight-loss/body-composition topic, which could mislead viewers into thinking the video is about heart health, diluting its relevance and clarity. #0 offers the best mix of honest curiosity, emotional pull and topical fit.

issues.claim: From the SURMOUNT-1 body-scan substudy (160 adults, DXA scans, 72 weeks, tirzepatide doses pooled)
issues.problem: Shortens the trial population to 'adults'. The craft rules require the full SURMOUNT-1 population in pinned comments, and earlier pinned comments were flagged for this same shortening.
issues.fix: From the SURMOUNT-1 body-scan substudy (160 adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes; DXA scans; 72 weeks; tirzepatide doses pooled): about three-quarters of the weight lost was fat and about a quarter was lean mass, on tirzepatide and placebo alike. Lean mass isn't just muscle, and strength wasn't measured. Save this for your next prescriber visit. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

issues.problem: The closing narration says 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description', but the link goes to the channel home page, not a specific video. That's a small broken promise.
issues.fix: Replace the line with the full URL of the specific follow-up video, e.g. 'Watch next: youtube.com/watch?v=<VIDEO_ID>' using the real published ID. If no follow-up video is live yet, change the line to 'More explainers: youtube.com/@InforMedLab' and note it in the post notes.
